analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks under $50 billion in assets from direct CFPB supervision.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have freed banks and credit unions with up to $50 billion in assets from direct Consumer Financial Protection Bureau examinations, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on June 29, 2017 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau directly examines and requires reporting from banks and credit unions with $10 billion or more in assets. This bill would have raised that cutoff to $50 billion, so hundreds of mid-sized institutions would no longer face direct CFPB on-site supervision or regular consumer-protection reporting. The Bureau would still be able to enforce consumer laws against them, but would lose its routine window into their practices. The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions holding between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets. They would be spared the cost and disruption of direct CFPB examinations and the burden of routine reporting, while remaining fully subject to other federal banking regulators.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold for direct CFPB examination and supervision from $10 billion to $50 billion under section 1025 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act.
Raises the asset threshold for CFPB reporting requirements from $10 billion to $50 billion under section 1026, so institutions between the old and new cutoffs would stop filing the required reports.
The changes would take effect 45 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who bank with mid-sized institutions. The CFPB would lose routine, on-site examination and regular reporting from banks in the $10 billion to $50 billion range, leaving problems to surface mainly through complaints and enforcement after the fact rather than through proactive oversight.

drawbacks.text: Removing direct CFPB examinations means the Bureau would no longer routinely inspect the mortgage, credit card, and other consumer operations of banks between $10 billion and $50 billion, relying instead on complaints and after-the-fact enforcement.

Mid-sized banks are large enough to be systemic in local markets: a bank with $49 billion in assets is five times the size that Dodd-Frank's drafters set as the line for direct supervision, so the change is a large exemption rather than a modest tailoring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim was to reduce regulatory burden, and compliance with examinations does cost mid-sized banks real money. But the cost falls on the public side of the ledger: consumers would lose proactive federal oversight of exactly the institutions large enough to harm many customers, and smaller would only find problems through slow complaint-driven enforcement. The exemption is broad relative to the burden it removes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on June 29, 2017, and the committee never took it up before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Toomey introduced the bill on June 29, 2017, joined by Sen. Joe Donnelly as cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was recorded before the 115th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the existing CFPB examination and reporting rules covering banks above $10 billion, since the exemption never became law. Mid-sized banks, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, who kept current bank oversight

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the CFPB examination and reporting thresholds from $10 billion to $50 billion.

for.name: Sen. Joe Donnelly
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana; sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support never had a chance to show.

industries.industry: Mid-sized banks and credit unions ($10–$50 billion in assets)
industries.note: They would have been freed from direct CFPB examinations and routine consumer-protection reporting, saving compliance costs. The saving comes out of oversight of their own consumer practices, which is where customers would bear the risk.
Unaffected directly — still above even the proposed threshold — but a lighter-supervision precedent for mid-sized banks could strengthen arguments for easing their own requirements.
